name: QUIC & HTTP/3: 0-RTT Handshakes, Stream Multiplexing & Connection Migration
tagline: Eliminate TCP head-of-line blocking and dropped mobile connections with UDP-based multiplexed streams, 0-RTT TLS 1.3, and Connection ID migration.
purpose: Master QUIC and HTTP/3 transport mechanics—independent stream framing, 0-RTT anti-replay guards, Connection ID migration, and UDP GSO/eBPF scaling.

spark.summary: QUIC + HTTP/3 moves multiplexed streaming and TLS 1.3 into user-space over UDP, isolating packet loss per stream and surviving Wi-Fi-to-5G IP changes via Connection IDs.
spark.keyTakeaway: When cross-zone coordination becomes the latency bottleneck, stream Multiplexing &, decoupling streams from TCP's single ordered buffer and binding connections to cryptographic Connection IDs instead of 4-tuple IPs cuts mobile tail latency and eliminates connection drops.
spark.byteSummary:
HTTP/2 solved head-of-line (HOL) blocking at the application layer by multiplexing many logical streams over a single TCP connection, but it left a fatal bottleneck underneath: TCP itself enforces a strict, in-order byte stream. When a single packet carrying Stream 1 bytes is dropped on a lossy mobile network, the OS kernel TCP receive buffer stalls delivery of Streams 2 and 3 until that lost packet is retransmitted and acknowledged—even though Streams 2 and 3 arrived intact.

QUIC (RFC 9000) and HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) move transport framing, loss recovery, and TLS 1.3 encryption into user-space over UDP. Each HTTP/3 stream owns an independent ordered byte offset inside QUIC STREAM frames, so packet loss on Stream 1 pauses only Stream 1 while Streams 2 and 3 continue delivering frames immediately. Furthermore, QUIC integrates TLS 1.3 directly into the transport handshake (1-RTT cold start, 0-RTT session resumption) and decouples connection identity from the 4-tuple (src_ip, src_port, dst_ip, dst_port) via an explicit 64-bit Connection ID (CID).

Key trade-offs center on UDP middlebox traversal, CPU encryption overhead without kernel-offload GRO/GSO, and security guardrails: unverified UDP source addresses require a 3x amplification limit before address validation, and 0-RTT early data is replayable and must be restricted strictly to idempotent GET/HEAD requests or protected by anti-replay strike registers.

learningJourney.title: Why TCP + HTTP/2 Suffers Transport Head-of-Line Blocking
learningJourney.purpose: Contrast HTTP/2's single-TCP byte stream bottleneck against QUIC's independent per-stream framing over UDP.

explanation.foundation: Assuming a single TCP connection carries 3 concurrent HTTP/2 streams, TCP views all bytes as one opaque, strictly ordered stream. If packet #42 (belonging to Stream 1) is lost, packets #43 and #44 (Streams 2 and 3) sit trapped in the kernel's out-of-order receive queue for an entire RTT + retransmission delay.
explanation.core: QUIC replaces TCP's monolithic byte stream with independent STREAM frames multiplexed over UDP datagrams. Each UDP packet is decrypted and processed independently; losing packet #42 blocks only Stream 1's reassembly buffer while Streams 2 and 3 deliver data immediately.
explanation.deepDive: At 2% packet loss (common on congested LTE/5G), HTTP/3 cuts p99 page-load tail latency by 25-40% compared to HTTP/2 over TCP, and uses QPACK (instead of HPACK) so dynamic header-table updates never stall unrelated streams.

sectionDiagram.title: Why TCP + HTTP/2 Suffers Transport Head-of-Line Blocking

cards.label: Kernel TCP Constraint
cards.detail: The OS TCP stack has no visibility into HTTP/2 stream IDs, forcing all streams to wait on any single gap.

cards.label: Independent Framing
cards.detail: QUIC decodes each UDP datagram independently in user space and delivers intact streams immediately.

cards.label: QPACK Header Safety
cards.detail: HTTP/3 replaces HPACK with QPACK to avoid header-compression HOL blocking across streams.

sectionDiagram.summary: QUIC eliminates TCP head-of-line blocking by isolating packet loss to the affected stream instead of stalling all multiplexed requests.
sectionDiagram.caption: QUIC eliminates TCP head-of-line blocking by isolating packet loss to the affected stream instead of stalling all multiplexed requests.

learningJourney.title: Merged TLS 1.3 Transport Handshake & 0-RTT Resumption
learningJourney.purpose: Reduce cold connection setup to 1-RTT and warm resumptions to 0-RTT while guarding against replay attacks.

explanation.foundation: TCP + TLS 1.3 requires 1 RTT for TCP SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK followed by 1-2 RTTs for TLS negotiation before encrypted HTTP bytes flow. QUIC embeds TLS 1.3 CRYPTO frames directly inside the Initial UDP packet, completing both transport and crypto setup in 1 RTT.
explanation.core: For returning clients holding a session ticket, QUIC allows 0-RTT early data to ride alongside the Initial handshake packet. Because a network attacker can capture and replay that first UDP datagram, 0-RTT MUST never carry non-idempotent mutations (like POST /pay).
explanation.deepDive: Production servers enforce a strict replay window (e.g., 10s ticket age tolerance) paired with a distributed Bloom/strike register keyed by the 0-RTT obfuscated ticket nonce, rejecting replays with HTTP 425 Too Early.

sectionDiagram.title: Merged TLS 1.3 Transport Handshake & 0-RTT Resumption

cards.label: Combined Handshake
cards.detail: Transport parameters and TLS 1.3 key exchange complete in a single round-trip.

cards.label: 0-RTT Replay Risk
cards.detail: Attackers can replay the initial 0-RTT UDP datagram; restrict 0-RTT strictly to idempotent reads.

cards.label: HTTP 425 Too Early
cards.detail: If a 0-RTT ticket is replayed or arrives outside the clock window, return 425 so the client retries in 1-RTT.

sectionDiagram.summary: Merging TLS 1.3 into QUIC Initial packets achieves 1-RTT cold setup and 0-RTT resumption guarded by anti-replay registers.
sectionDiagram.caption: Merging TLS 1.3 into QUIC Initial packets achieves 1-RTT cold setup and 0-RTT resumption guarded by anti-replay registers.

decisionFramework.problem: How to implement QUIC & HTTP/3: 0-RTT Handshakes, Stream Multiplexing & Connection Migration without hitting unbounded tail latency, state divergence, or operational fragility.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Use a single unpartitioned path with unbounded retries and synchronous global coordination.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Global coordination serializes throughput under load, while unbounded retries amplify transient stalls into full outages.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Compare synchronous strict-consistency paths against bounded asynchronous replication, local caching, or partitioned ownership.
decisionFramework.decision: When cross-zone coordination becomes the latency bottleneck, stream Multiplexing &, decoupling streams from TCP's single ordered buffer and binding connections to cryptographic Connection IDs instead of 4-tuple IPs cuts mobile tail latency and eliminates connection drops.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Gains predictable p99 latency and fault isolation in exchange for explicit bounding, observability, and slightly higher implementation complexity.

learningJourney.title: 64-Bit Connection IDs & Seamless Wi-Fi-to-5G Migration
learningJourney.purpose: Keep active streams alive across client IP and NAT port changes using cryptographic Connection IDs and PATH_CHALLENGE.

explanation.foundation: A TCP connection is permanently bound to its 4-tuple (src_ip, src_port, dst_ip, dst_port). Walking out of Wi-Fi onto 5G breaks every active TCP socket, forcing slow DNS/TCP/TLS reconnects and aborted uploads.
explanation.core: QUIC identifies connections by an explicit Connection ID (CID) in the short packet header. When a phone switches from Wi-Fi to 5G, it keeps sending encrypted packets with the same server CID from its new IP.
explanation.deepDive: To prevent off-path attackers from spoofing a peer's IP migration (traffic redirection attack), the server issues a 64-bit random PATH_CHALLENGE frame to the new address and switches congestion-control state only after receiving PATH_RESPONSE.

sectionDiagram.title: 64-Bit Connection IDs & Seamless Wi-Fi-to-5G Migration

cards.label: CID Decoupling
cards.detail: Connections survive Wi-Fi/5G switches and carrier NAT rebinding without re-handshaking.

cards.label: Linkability Defense
cards.detail: Clients rotate to a fresh pre-issued NEW_CONNECTION_ID on migration so passive observers cannot track IPs.

cards.label: Congestion Reset
cards.detail: Reset cwnd and RTT estimates on the new path because 5G bandwidth differs from Wi-Fi.

sectionDiagram.summary: Explicit Connection IDs and PATH_CHALLENGE validation keep streams alive across Wi-Fi-to-5G handoffs without IP tracking.
sectionDiagram.caption: Explicit Connection IDs and PATH_CHALLENGE validation keep streams alive across Wi-Fi-to-5G handoffs without IP tracking.

learningJourney.title: 3x Amplification Guard & Replay-Safe 0-RTT Admission
learningJourney.purpose: Enforce RFC 9000's 3x unvalidated-address byte cap and reject replayed or non-idempotent 0-RTT requests.

explanation.foundation: Because UDP lacks TCP's 3-way handshake, a spoofed client IP could trick a QUIC server into sending huge TLS certificates to a victim. RFC 9000 mandates that servers send at most 3x the bytes received from an unvalidated address.
explanation.deepDive: Padding Client Initial packets to at least 1,200 bytes gives the server a 3,600-byte unvalidated budget—enough to return its Initial + Handshake certificate chain without stalling.

sectionDiagram.title: 3x Amplification Guard & Replay-Safe 0-RTT Admission

cards.label: 3x Amplification Rule
cards.detail: Never send >3x received bytes before address validation completes via Handshake ACK or RETRY token.

cards.label: 1,200-Byte Minimum
cards.detail: Drop unpadded Client Initials <1,200 bytes so servers aren't forced to fragment handshake replies.

cards.label: Fail-Closed 0-RTT
cards.detail: Return HTTP 425 Too Early on non-idempotent verbs or duplicate ticket nonces.

sectionDiagram.summary: Enforcing the 3x unvalidated byte limit and 425 Too Early anti-replay checks prevents UDP amplification and duplicate mutations.
sectionDiagram.caption: Enforcing the 3x unvalidated byte limit and 425 Too Early anti-replay checks prevents UDP amplification and duplicate mutations.

learningJourney.title: Closing the UDP CPU Gap with GSO, GRO & eBPF CID Routing
learningJourney.purpose: Cut user-space QUIC syscall overhead using UDP GSO/GRO batching and stateless eBPF Connection-ID routing.

explanation.foundation: Naive user-space QUIC calls sendmsg()/recvmsg() once per 1,200-byte UDP packet, burning 2-3x more CPU than kernel TCP with TSO/GRO.
explanation.core: Modern Linux kernels (5.0+) support UDP_SEGMENT (GSO) and UDP_GRO, allowing user-space QUIC stacks to pass 64 KB batches in one syscall while the NIC segments/coalesces packets in hardware.
explanation.deepDive: At L4 load balancers, ECMP hashing on the 4-tuple breaks whenever a mobile client migrates IPs. Embedding a 16-bit Server ID inside the QUIC CID lets stateless eBPF/XDP load balancers route packets consistently regardless of client IP.

sectionDiagram.title: Closing the UDP CPU Gap with GSO, GRO & eBPF CID Routing

cards.label: Syscall Batching
cards.detail: UDP GSO/GRO cuts kernel-userspace context switches by ~40x on bulk HTTP/3 downloads.

cards.label: Stateless L4 Routing
cards.detail: Routing by embedded Server-ID bits in the CID preserves stickiness across IP migrations without shared state.

cards.label: PACING / BBRv2
cards.detail: User-space pacing spreads bursts evenly instead of dumping 50-packet GSO trains into shallow Wi-Fi buffers.

sectionDiagram.summary: UDP GSO/GRO batching and eBPF Connection-ID routing match TCP throughput while keeping mobile migrations sticky.
sectionDiagram.caption: UDP GSO/GRO batching and eBPF Connection-ID routing match TCP throughput while keeping mobile migrations sticky.

learningJourney.title: Happy Eyeballs v2 Fallback for Blocked UDP/443 Networks
learningJourney.purpose: Isolate corporate firewalls that drop UDP/443 by racing HTTP/3 against HTTP/2 over TCP without user-visible stalls.

explanation.foundation: Roughly 3-7% of enterprise firewalls and hotel captive portals drop or rate-limit UDP port 443, which would hang a QUIC-only client.
explanation.core: Browsers advertise HTTP/3 via the `Alt-Svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400` header or HTTPS DNS records, and race QUIC against TCP+TLS using a 50-100 ms Happy Eyeballs head-start timer.
explanation.deepDive: If UDP/443 fails or stalls twice consecutively on a network, the client caches a negative Alt-Svc cooldown for that Wi-Fi SSID and serves HTTP/2 over TCP immediately.

sectionDiagram.title: Happy Eyeballs v2 Fallback for Blocked UDP/443 Networks

cards.label: Never QUIC-Only
cards.detail: Always maintain an HTTP/2 over TCP fallback path on port 443 for restrictive enterprise networks.

cards.label: Short Race Delay
cards.detail: A 50-100 ms head start prevents wasted TCP handshakes on healthy networks while bounding worst-case fallback.

cards.label: Per-Network Memory
cards.detail: Scope negative QUIC cache entries to network SSID/BSSID so switching to 5G re-enables HTTP/3.

sectionDiagram.summary: Happy Eyeballs racing and per-SSID negative caching insulate users from UDP-blocking firewalls with zero hangs.
sectionDiagram.caption: Happy Eyeballs racing and per-SSID negative caching insulate users from UDP-blocking firewalls with zero hangs.

learningJourney.title: Tracking QUIC Loss, 0-RTT Rejections & CID Migration Health
learningJourney.purpose: Monitor encrypted QUIC connections via QLOG traces, 425 replay rates, and fallback ratios.

explanation.foundation: Because QUIC encrypts transport headers (packet numbers, ACKs, stream IDs), passive network taps like tcpdump cannot inspect retransmissions.
explanation.core: Production stacks emit structured **QLOG** event streams from the endpoints themselves, tracking packet loss, spin-bit RTT, 0-RTT acceptance vs. 425 rejections, and CID migration success.
explanation.deepDive: Alert whenever HTTP/3 fallback-to-TCP rate spikes above 10% (indicating regional ISP UDP throttling) or when unvalidated 3x amplification drops climb during DDoS floods.

sectionDiagram.title: Tracking QUIC Loss, 0-RTT Rejections & CID Migration Health

cards.label: No Passive Tcpdump
cards.detail: QUIC encrypts ACK/sequence metadata—endpoint QLOG sampling is mandatory for transport debugging.

cards.label: Regional UDP Alerts
cards.detail: Spike in H3->H2 fallback by ASN pinpoints carrier UDP shaping immediately.

cards.label: 0-RTT Replay Spikes
cards.detail: Sudden 425 surges indicate either replay attacks or clock skew across edge PoPs.

sectionDiagram.summary: Sampled endpoint QLOG telemetry, 425 replay ratios, and ASN fallback alerts make encrypted QUIC observable.
sectionDiagram.caption: Sampled endpoint QLOG telemetry, 425 replay ratios, and ASN fallback alerts make encrypted QUIC observable.

knowledgeChecks.question: A mobile client downloads 3 parallel assets over HTTP/2 (TCP) vs. HTTP/3 (QUIC). Packet #19 belonging exclusively to Stream 1 is dropped. What happens to Streams 2 and 3?

options.text: Both HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 stall Streams 2 and 3 until packet #19 is retransmitted.
options.feedback: Only TCP stalls all streams; QUIC delivers Stream 2 and 3 frames independently.

options.text: HTTP/2 stalls Streams 2 and 3 in the TCP receive buffer, whereas HTTP/3 delivers Streams 2 and 3 immediately.
options.feedback: Correct! TCP enforces one global byte order, whereas QUIC isolates loss per STREAM frame.

options.text: HTTP/3 drops Streams 2 and 3 permanently because UDP is unreliable.
options.feedback: QUIC implements per-stream reliability and retransmission on top of UDP.

options.text: HTTP/2 continues Streams 2 and 3 because HPACK separates stream buffers.
options.feedback: HPACK is application-layer; the kernel TCP buffer still blocks all upper streams on any gap.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: TCP enforces strict in-order byte delivery across the whole socket, while QUIC tracks offsets independently per stream.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must an HTTP/3 edge gateway reject `POST /api/v1/transfer` sent inside QUIC 0-RTT early data with HTTP 425 Too Early?

options.text: 0-RTT packets are unencrypted and expose JSON payloads.
options.feedback: 0-RTT data is encrypted with the resumption PSK; the risk is replayability, not plaintext.

options.text: 0-RTT only supports UDP payloads smaller than 256 bytes.
options.feedback: 0-RTT has no 256-byte limit; it is constrained by the 3x amplification cap and replay safety.

options.text: An attacker can capture and replay the initial 0-RTT UDP datagram before the handshake completes, causing duplicate state mutations.
options.feedback: Correct! Because 0-RTT lacks fresh server-contributed entropy, it is replayable and must be restricted to idempotent requests.

options.text: 0-RTT requires a separate TCP fallback socket for POST bodies.
options.feedback: POST requests simply wait 1 RTT for the handshake to complete over the same QUIC connection.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: 0-RTT early data lacks fresh server randomness and can be replayed by an on-path attacker, so non-idempotent mutations must be rejected with 425 Too Early.

knowledgeChecks.question: When a mobile user walks from office Wi-Fi onto 5G cellular, why does an active QUIC connection survive without re-handshaking?

options.text: QUIC connections are identified by an explicit Connection ID (CID) in the header rather than the client's IP:Port 4-tuple.
options.feedback: Correct! Explicit CIDs plus PATH_CHALLENGE/PATH_RESPONSE let the server migrate the connection to the new 5G IP seamlessly.

options.text: The mobile OS keeps the old Wi-Fi IP address active inside the 5G tunnel forever.
options.feedback: Client source IP and NAT port change when switching interfaces.

options.text: UDP sockets automatically broadcast packets to all nearby cell towers.
options.feedback: Migration relies on explicit CIDs and return-routability validation, not broadcast.

options.text: QUIC disables TLS encryption during cellular handoffs.
options.feedback: All migrated packets remain fully AEAD-encrypted and authenticated.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Decoupling connection identity from the 4-tuple via cryptographic Connection IDs allows seamless migration across network interfaces.
